title: Losar again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirvana Day: a fire gone out, a doctor who seemed to leave, a coming and going that was neither. Your line was all things end. What did you finish on purpose? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

A guest steps into a Tibetan home on new year's morning, and before anything else, someone holds out a wooden box. It's split in two. One side is heaped with roasted barley flour, the other with barley grain, and stalks of grain stand up out of it like little flags. The guest takes a pinch and tosses it into the air, takes another and tosses it again, a third time, then puts a pinch on the tongue. Then the greetings begin. This is Losar, and you've met its brooms and prayer flags before. Today, look at it with the Tibetan map from this year in hand.
screen: `A BOX OF BARLEY.` → `A PINCH TOSSED UP.` → `A PINCH TASTED.`

segments.voice: Back in the Tibetan block, you met a way Tibetan teachers describe their path: three vehicles practiced together, not one after another. Renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path. Losar isn't a teaching on that map, and nobody needs to treat it as one. But here's one way to walk through the festival with it. First, letting go. In the last days of the old year, houses are scrubbed, and old dust and old troubles are carried out the door. That's the household version of renunciation: the old year is really over, so you stop holding it. Second, sharing. The pinch of barley isn't kept. It's thrown up and out, an offering, before anyone eats. Then come the visits, the gifts, the greeting tashi delek, wishing good fortune on whoever you meet. The fresh year starts by giving something away. Third, the diamond path. In the monasteries, the turn of the year brings rituals and chanting, and in some places masked dances. And in the first month, by tradition, comes the Great Prayer festival, Monlam Chenmo, which Tibetan histories say Tsongkhapa, the founder of the Gelug school you met this year, began in Lhasa. Monks gather to pray for the world, and lay people come to offer lamps and food. Its name, monlam, means an aspiration prayer: a wish set out ahead of you. So the year begins with all three at once. Clear the corner. Throw the pinch. Set out the wish. None of them waits for the others to be finished, which is just what those teachers said about the vehicles.
screen: `THREE VEHICLES, PRACTICED TOGETHER.` · `LETTING GO: THE SCRUBBED HOUSE.` · `SHARING: THE PINCH THROWN UP.` · then, large: `THE WISH: THE GREAT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: clean one corner. You can do the cleaning later. For now, sit, and picture the corner. One shelf, one drawer, one spot by the door. With a few breaths, see what's there from a year that's already over, and let yourself decide what goes. Then, with the next few breaths, think of one person who might use something you'd let go of. And with the last few, set out one wish for the coming year, short and plain, as if you were writing it on a flag for the wind. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Losar. The Tibetan new year: houses cleaned, offerings shared, and in the monasteries, rituals and the Great Prayer. Today's word.
Your line: a fresh year. Today, clean your corner, give away one thing from it, and say your wish once, out loud or under your breath. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Tibetans and Himalayan Buddhist communities keep Losar by the lunar calendar with house cleaning, new prayer flags, family visits, offerings of barley flour and grain, and monastery rituals; in the first month, monasteries in some places also hold Monlam prayer gatherings.

Hook describes the chemar (phye mar) box: tsampa on one side, barley grain on the other, stalks standing up; guest tosses a pinch three times and tastes a pinch. Customs vary by region; please confirm.
The three-vehicle reading of Losar is the writer's framing, stated in the script as 'one way to walk through the festival', not as a tradition's teaching. A Keeper may prefer to soften or remove it.
Monlam Chenmo: Tibetan histories credit Tsongkhapa with founding it in Lhasa; no date given per the claims rule. Confirm 'in the first month' and the description of lay offerings.
Masked dances at the new year: monastery practice varies; confirm the general phrasing.
Original: Tibetan smon lam (སྨོན་ལམ་); confirm spelling and the pronunciation guide.
Editor: cut 'in great numbers' (count claim) from Monlam; masked dances now 'around the turn of the year, in some places' since they precede Losar and vary by monastery.
